## Overview

Backpressure is a fundamental mechanism in streaming and data pipeline systems that allows a slow downstream consumer to signal an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate. Without backpressure, an unbounded buffer can grow between producer and consumer, eventually exhausting available memory and crashing the system.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues with Blocking

The producer writes to a bounded queue (fixed size). Once the queue is full, the producer is blocked—prevented from writing—until the consumer removes items, freeing space. This is the simplest form of backpressure and is common in single-threaded or thread-pool architectures.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

In this model, the consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send up to N additional items (a "credit"). As the producer emits items, it consumes credits; when credits are exhausted, the producer stops. The consumer replenishes credits as it processes items. This approach works well in asynchronous, distributed systems where explicit permission is clearer than implicit blocking.

### Reactive-Pull Model

Instead of the producer pushing items on its own schedule, the consumer pulls (requests) items on demand. The consumer decides when to request more data, giving it direct control over the rate of emission. This is the model used by reactive streams frameworks (e.g., Reactive Streams specification, RxJava) and is particularly effective for handling heterogeneous processing speeds.

## Significance

Backpressure is essential for building robust, memory-efficient streaming systems. Without it, systems are vulnerable to:
- Unbounded memory growth
- Out-of-memory errors
- Loss of data when buffers overflow
- Cascading failures in pipelines with multiple stages
